title: Act III, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Banquo suspects Macbeth 'play'dst most foully' for the crown but hopes the prophecy for his own line will also come true. Macbeth, now king, invites Banquo to the feast and learns he will ride out with Fleance. Alone, Macbeth says 'To be thus is nothing; but to be safely thus': Banquo's royal nature and the prophecy of his heirs torment him, since he holds a 'fruitless crown.' He persuades two murderers that Banquo is their enemy and hires them to kill Banquo and Fleance.

context.history: Because James I claimed descent from Banquo, Shakespeare makes Banquo noble, departing from Holinshed, where Banquo helps kill Duncan.

significance: Getting the crown has not ended Macbeth's ambition; it has turned it into fear. He now plots without his wife, manipulating the murderers as she manipulated him.
discussionQuestions: Once someone gets what they wanted, why are they sometimes still unhappy?

anchorPassages.text:
But to be safely thus.—Our fears in Banquo
Stick deep; and in his royalty of nature
Reigns that which would be fear’d: ’tis much he dares;
And, to that dauntless temper of his mind,
He hath a wisdom that doth guide his valour
To act in safety. There is none but he
Whose being I do fear: and, under him,
My Genius is rebuked; as, it is said,
Mark Antony’s was by Caesar. He chid the sisters
When first they put the name of king upon me,
And bade them speak to him: then prophet-like
They hail’d him father to a line of kings:
Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown,
And put a barren sceptre in my gripe,
Thence to be wrench’d with an unlineal hand,
No son of mine succeeding. If’t be so,
For Banquo’s issue have I filed my mind;
For them the gracious Duncan have I murder’d;
Put rancours in the vessel of my peace
Only for them; and mine eternal jewel
Given to the common enemy of man,
To make them kings, the seed of Banquo kings!
Rather than so, come fate into the list,
And champion me to the utterance! Who’s there!

segments.activity: Five key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Today's words: buffets — blows; hard knocks; predominant — strongest; ruling over the rest; parricide — the murder of one's father; disasters — misfortunes; rebuked — checked; held back. “parricide”: Origin: possibly Middle French parricide; earlier Latin parricīda. “disasters”: Origin of “disaster”: Middle French desastre; earlier Latin astrum (“star”).

words.sentence:
I am one, my liege,
Whom the vile blows and buffets of the world
Have so incensed that I am reckless what
I do to spite the world.

Do you find
Your patience so predominant in your nature
That you can let this go?

We hear, our bloody cousins are bestow’d
In England and in Ireland, not confessing
Their cruel parricide, filling their hearers
With strange invention: but of that to-morrow,
When therewithal we shall have cause of state
Craving us jointly.

And I another
So weary with disasters, tugg’d with fortune,
That I would set my life on any chance,
To mend it, or be rid on’t.

There is none but he
Whose being I do fear: and, under him,
My Genius is rebuked; as, it is said,
Mark Antony’s was by Caesar.

wordHistories: “parricide”: Origin: possibly Middle French parricide; earlier Latin parricīda.
“disasters”: Origin of “disaster”: Middle French desastre; earlier Latin astrum (“star”).

segments.script: Because James I claimed descent from Banquo, Shakespeare makes Banquo noble, departing from Holinshed, where Banquo helps kill Duncan. Getting the crown has not ended Macbeth's ambition; it has turned it into fear. He now plots without his wife, manipulating the murderers as she manipulated him. Soliloquy: "To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus": Macbeth fears Banquo and his heirs. Characterization: Macbeth hires murderers by manipulating them, using Lady Macbeth's tactic of attacking manhood. Imagery: "Fruitless crown" and "barren sceptre": he has no heir. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus” slowly and put it in my own words: Macbeth says that being king is nothing unless he is safely king. Next, craft. I notice the contrast between "thus" and "safely thus." The strongest word is “safely”: it shows his new anxiety about keeping power. Then, effect. Why is being king not enough for Macbeth? My answer: Being king is not enough for Macbeth because he is not safe; his crown brings fear, not peace, so he decides to kill Banquo, whose descendants the witches said would be kings.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

lessonAtAGlance.title: Act III, Scene I
lessonAtAGlance.objective: Students will analyze how characterization develops in “Act III, Scene I” by writing a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that cites at least 2 quotations from the section, and will score at least 80% on the section quiz.

readingChunk.minutesEstimate: about 8 minutes at 150 words a minute (estimate)

anchor.opening: Thou hast it now: king, Cawdor, Glamis, all,
anchor.closing: And set me up in hope? But hush! no more.

lessonAtAGlance.assessment: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket
